prompt: In a stack of screens, what does going back do?

choices.text: Goes to the root
choices.why: One press pops one screen. Going straight to the root is what a second tap on a tab does.

choices.text: Reloads the previous screen from the start, with its data fetched again
choices.why: The screen under the top one is kept as it was left; nothing reloads it.

choices.text: Pops the top screen; the one under it shows as it was left
choices.why: Right. That is a pop: the screen under it was never redrawn from scratch.

choices.text: Switches to the previous tab
choices.why: A stack has no tabs; switching tabs is a different shape.

prompt: A student is three screens deep in Courses, taps Week, then taps Courses. What should they see?

choices.text: The form they were on
choices.why: Right. Each tab keeps its own stack, so switching away and back leaves it where it was.

choices.text: The Courses list, because switching tabs starts each tab again
choices.why: That is the behaviour multiple back stacks exist to prevent.

choices.text: The Week screen, pushed on top of Courses
choices.why: That would be a single history list; tabs do not push onto each other.

choices.text: A blank screen until the app reloads its data
choices.why: Nothing about switching tabs empties a screen.

prompt: What does a tap on the tab that is already showing do, by the convention the lesson describes?

choices.text: Nothing; the tab is already open
choices.why: It does something: it is the one-tap way home inside that tab.

choices.text: Opens the drawer
choices.why: The drawer is a separate shape with its own control.

choices.text: Pops one screen, like back
choices.why: It goes further than one screen: all the way to the root.

choices.text: Takes that tab back to its root screen
choices.why: Right. Apple's tab bar controller and React Navigation's bottom tabs both do it.

prompt: The planner's new-session form is drawn as a sheet instead of a pushed screen. The student closes it. Where are they?

choices.text: At the root of Courses
choices.why: Closing a sheet does not touch the stack under it.

choices.text: Exactly where they were before it opened
choices.why: Right. A sheet never joins the stack it covers, so nothing under it moved.

choices.text: One screen further back than before it opened
choices.why: That would mean the sheet had popped something it never pushed.

choices.text: On the Week tab, which the sheet switched to
choices.why: A sheet has no say over which tab shows.

prompt: Match each shape to what back does in it.

pairs.right: dismisses it, leaving the screen under it as it was

prompt: Who provides the back action on an Android phone?

choices.text: Each app, as a button it draws
choices.why: That is iOS. On Android the system provides back and the app only decides what it does.

choices.text: The system, as a button or an edge swipe
choices.why: Right. The app cannot draw it or remove it.

choices.text: The navigation library the app chose
choices.why: The library answers back; the system is what sends it.

choices.text: The phone's manufacturer, only on some models
choices.why: Every Android phone has it; it is part of the system.

prompt: On Android 12 or later, a student presses back at the root of the planner's start tab. What happens to the app?

choices.text: It is killed at once, and everything the student had open is lost
choices.why: Since Android 12 the task is moved to the background rather than finished.

choices.text: Nothing; the press is ignored at the root
choices.why: That is closer to iOS, where the root simply has no back button.

choices.text: It asks the user to confirm before leaving
choices.why: No confirmation is part of the system's behaviour.

choices.text: Its task moves to the background, as with the Home gesture
choices.why: Right. Android's documentation on the Android 12 behaviour changes says so.

prompt: A link in a chat app opens the planner straight on one course. What does Android's up arrow do there?

choices.text: Goes to the Courses list
choices.why: Right, though the student never opened it. Up goes to the screen above in your app's hierarchy, through a stack built for the occasion.

choices.text: Returns to the chat app it came from
choices.why: That is what back does after a link from another app; up stays in your app.

choices.text: Closes the planner
choices.why: Up never exits the app, by Android's navigation principles.

choices.text: Nothing; up only appears on iOS
choices.why: Up is Android's arrow in the app bar; iOS's back button does both jobs.

prompt: Which of these are true of iOS? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Going back is a button the app draws, at the top left
choices.why: Right. iOS has no system back.

choices.text: A swipe from the left edge is a shortcut to that button
choices.why: Right. Apple's guidelines describe it as a shortcut offered while keeping the button.

choices.text: Back at the root of the app leaves it
choices.why: There is no back at the root on iOS; the person leaves with the system's home gesture.

choices.text: Every app must answer a system back gesture
choices.why: That is Android's rule, not iOS's.

prompt: Why does predictive back make an app declare in advance whether it will handle back itself?

choices.text: So that iOS can show the same animation
choices.why: Predictive back is Android's alone.

choices.text: Because back presses are counted for the store
choices.why: No store counts them; the reason is the animation.

choices.text: The system has to draw what is behind before the finger lifts
choices.why: Right. It previews the destination during the swipe, so the answer is needed before the press is over.

choices.text: Because back no longer exists on Android 15
choices.why: Back exists; from Android 15 its preview animations appear by default for apps that opted in.

prompt: In backstack.ts, why does open change only nav.stacks[nav.tab]?

choices.text: A screen opened in a tab belongs to that tab
choices.why: Right. That is the whole of each tab having its own stack.

choices.text: To save memory
choices.why: Memory is not the point; the copy is tiny either way.

choices.text: Because the other stack is read-only in TypeScript
choices.why: Nothing in the types makes it read-only; the rule is the design.

choices.text: Because only one tab at a time can ever hold any screens
choices.why: Both tabs hold screens; Week has session:s3 in the run.

prompt: What does back return when the student is at the root of START?

choices.text: An empty stack for Courses
choices.why: A root is never removed, so no stack ever becomes empty.

choices.text: A switch to Week
choices.why: Switching happens at the root of a tab that is not START; this is START.

choices.text: The same state, with left set to true
choices.why: Right. Nothing is left inside the app, and the caller learns that from left.

choices.text: An error thrown at the caller
choices.why: Leaving the app is an ordinary outcome, not a failure.

prompt: To add a sheet to the model, the lesson suggests a field sheet: string | null. In which order should back look at things?

choices.text: The stacks first, and the sheet only when every stack is at its root
choices.why: Then back would pop screens hidden under a sheet the student is looking at.

choices.text: The sheet first; only with none open, the stacks
choices.why: Right. What is on top is closed first, which is the order Android follows.

choices.text: Whichever of the two was opened first, sheet or screen
choices.why: Back undoes the most recent thing on top, not the oldest.

choices.text: It does not matter; the result is the same
choices.why: It matters: one order closes the sheet, the other moves the screen under it.

prompt: A tap on the tab already showing keeps only its root, with nav.stacks[tab].___(0, 1).
After the row `open new-session`, how many screens does the Courses stack hold?
On the row `tap Week`, the iOS back column reads no, though three screens are open in Courses. Why?

choices.text: iOS clears the other tab's stack on a switch
choices.why: The Courses stack is untouched in that row.

choices.text: iPhones never draw a back button inside tabs
choices.why: One row later, with session:s3 pushed on Week, it reads yes.

choices.text: backButton has a bug for the second tab
choices.why: It reads the stack of the tab showing, which is correct.

choices.text: Week is showing, and Week is at its root
choices.why: Right. The button belongs to the stack on screen, not to the session as a whole.

prompt: From `week > session:s3` on the Week tab, put Android's back presses in the order they act.
items: switch to Courses, the start tab

prompt: What does the second tap on Courses (row 8) do to the Week stack?

choices.text: Empties it
choices.why: No stack ever loses its root.

choices.text: Cuts it back to week
choices.why: Only the Courses stack is cut back.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The rule only touches the tab that was tapped; Week keeps session:s3.

choices.text: Pushes courses onto it
choices.why: Tabs never push onto each other.

prompt: The student is on new-session, three screens deep in Courses, the start tab. How many Android back presses until the app leaves?
If the planner had a single history list instead of a stack per tab, what would back from session:s3 have shown in the run?

choices.text: The new-session form in Courses
choices.why: Right. One list mixes the tabs, so back lands in the middle of the other tab.

choices.text: The Week screen
choices.why: In one list the screen before session:s3 is whatever was opened before it, and Week was switched to, not opened.

choices.text: The root of Courses
choices.why: One press pops one entry; the root is further back.

choices.text: The app would leave
choices.why: There are screens left in the list.

prompt: In Navigation Compose, what do saveState and restoreState do when the student switches tabs?

choices.text: Write the stack to disk for the next launch
choices.why: They keep a tab's stack between switches, in the running app.

choices.text: Turn on predictive back
choices.why: Predictive back is unrelated to tab switching.

choices.text: Make back leave the app from any tab
choices.why: They have nothing to do with what back does at a root.

choices.text: Keep the tab being left and bring back the one being opened
choices.why: Right. Without them every switch starts the tab again from its root.

prompt: Match each toolkit to the thing that holds a stack in it.
What does the lesson say about the Kotlin, Swift and React Native fragments?

choices.text: They were run on an Android emulator and on Apple's iOS simulator
choices.why: No emulator or simulator was used for this course.

choices.text: Adapted from documentation, never compiled or run here
choices.why: Right. They are for recognising the idea; the courses after the fork run them.

choices.text: They are complete apps
choices.why: They are fragments.

choices.text: They are the same code in three syntaxes

prompt: A team adds a drawer to the planner with five destinations. In backstack.ts terms, what is each destination?

choices.text: A screen pushed on top of the Courses stack, above the list
choices.why: A destination is a section with its own root, not a screen inside another section.

choices.text: Another key of stacks, like a tab with its bar hidden
choices.why: Right. The same model serves; only the control that switches differs.

choices.text: A sheet
choices.why: A sheet covers the current screen for one task; a drawer destination replaces the section.

choices.text: Nothing the model can hold
choices.why: The model holds it as one more stack.

prompt: Which part of navigation is a constraint the system enforces, rather than a design convention?

choices.text: Where the tab bar sits on the screen, at the bottom or the top
choices.why: That is a convention the guidelines describe.

choices.text: Using a drawer instead of tabs
choices.why: Also a design choice, with its own cost.

choices.text: Whether the new-session form is a sheet
choices.why: That is a design choice.

choices.text: Android's system back, which every app has to answer
choices.why: Right. The app cannot remove it, only decide what it does.
